items.titel: Five EU countries tout Rwanda deportation partnership, but no formal deal as key details remain secret
items.anriss: Rejected asylum seekers with deportation orders from possibly even as far away as Afghanistan may end up in Rwanda, following the announcement of talks spearheaded by five European countries with Kigali on Monday (16 November).

absaetze.t: Rejected asylum seekers with deportation orders from possibly even as far away as Afghanistan may end up in Rwanda, following the announcement of talks spearheaded by five European countries with Kigali on Monday (16 November).

No formal deal has been signed, posing questions on why Austria’s chancellor Christian Stocker and Denmark’s prime minister Mette Frederiksen, along ministers from Austria, Germany, Greece, the Netherlands and Rwanda’s interior minister Vincent Biruta, would announce anything.

Instead, they gathered in Vienna, held a press conference and told journalists that a “partnership” had been agreed with Rwanda amid outstanding technical issues that still need to be sorted in the hopes of signing a formal deal in the coming months.

The plan is to start deportations next year, said Austria’s Stocker despite Rwanda’s checkered human rights spanning political repression to its support of the M23 armed group operating in the eastern DR Congo.
Even so Stocker described it as a “truly historic paradigm”, noting that Austria had deported more people than it has had asylum applications.
His comments were largely echoed by Frederiksen, who said they now have a broad majority of European countries for a more sustainable migration policy.

"We are now ready to move into more concrete steps," said Frederiksen, who claimed they intend to remove incentives for "illegal migration" by sending a global signal that they are not welcomed in Europe.
Little detail
Nobody would cite potential costs when pressed on specifics.
Rwanda's Biruta said those received in Rwanda would have the opportunity to voluntarily continue home, go somewhere else, or integrate with legal residence and get jobs.

He cited Rwanda's experience of working with the International Organisation for Migration (IOM), a UN offshoot that flies in refugees stranded in Libya to a Rwandan hosted transit centre before being resettled elsewhere.
"We are sensitive to people who are seeking asylum. This is our main motivation," he said. "We are not looking at really getting money," he said amid promises that people would not be put in camps.

items.titel: Aux États-Unis, les plus grands data centers émettent déjà autant de CO₂ que le Danemark ou la Bolivie
items.anriss: Une étude de Harvard, publiée dans “Nature Sustainability”, chiffre pour la première fois depuis l’essor de l’IA l’électricité engloutie par les “hyperscalers” américains, ces centres de données géants gérés dans l’opacité.

absaetze.t: Les plus grands data centers des États-Unis rejettent chaque année quelque 25,7 millions de tonnes de CO₂, “presque autant que des pays entiers comme la Bolivie ou le Danemark”, rapporte The New York Times.

Publiée lundi 16 novembre dans Nature Sustainability, l’étude conduite par une équipe de Harvard, a passé au crible 403 installations américaines entre mai 2024 et avril 2025. À elles seules, elles ont absorbé près de 2 % de l’électricité du pays, davantage que New York et Los Angeles réunies, et plus de la moitié de l’électricité qui les alimente provient de la combustion de gaz naturel et de charbon. Trois États, la Virginie, l’Iowa et l’Ohio concentrent environ la moitié des émissions.

Le quotidien new-yorkais souligne que ces résultats relèvent d’un “travail de détective” : faute de registre public, les chercheurs ont dû scruter des images satellites pour localiser les bâtiments et en évaluer la taille et la consommation. Ce qui “en dit long sur le manque de transparence qui règne dans ce secteur”, assène Gianluca Guidi, le scientifique de Harvard qui a dirigé l’équipe de recherche.

Cette opacité nourrit en outre la défiance des citoyens, constate le journal de centre gauche : lors des dernières élections de mi-mandat, les électeurs ont ainsi choisi “de limiter ou d’empêcher ces implantations dans 40 des 41 référendums locaux portant sur le sujet”.
Peu d’études sur le sujet

The Washington Post s’attarde sur la nature de ces “hyperscalers”, “les plus grands et les plus énergivores” des centres de données, ceux qui servent à entraîner et à faire tourner l’intelligence artificielle. Leurs émissions, relève le journal de la capitale, sont “deux à trois fois supérieures” à celles de la dernière évaluation, qui remontait à 2018.

Leur consommation “approche celle d’un petit pays européen”, y résume Francesca Dominici, coautrice de l’étude, avant de s’interroger : “Cela pose la question de savoir si nous sommes sur la bonne trajectoire.”

Pour donner la mesure du phénomène, Fast Company convoque, pour sa part, la géographie américaine : avec 68 à 99 térawattheures engloutis en un an, ce parc consomme “autant d’électricité, voire plus, que des États entiers” − l’Indiana, le Michigan ou le Tennessee tournant par exemple chacun autour de 100.

Le magazine économique rappelle que la science sur les émissions des centres de données reste “rare”, et que les chercheurs eux-mêmes ont été “surpris” par leurs résultats. Lesquels sont déjà datés, tant les chantiers se sont multipliés depuis un an, souligne-t-il également.
En deçà de la réalité

Cette “construction frénétique”, alimentée par de nouvelles centrales à gaz, a beau être défendue par Donald Trump, qui promet aux opposants de finir “arriérés et pauvres”, elle se heurte à une “fronde transpartisane” qui “ne montre guère de signes d’essoufflement”, observe The Guardian.

Le quotidien britannique en suit la trace de Memphis, où les installations d’Elon Musk sont visées par des manifestations et des procès, jusqu’à l’Utah, où le gigantesque projet Stratos inquiète pour sa consommation d’eau. “La pollution provenant de Stratos contaminera l’air et compromettra la possibilité de vivre une vie saine aussi bien aux alentours du site que dans les États situés à des centaines de kilomètres du centre de données”, alerte John Walke, du Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), l’ONG qui a commandé un rapport sur le projet.

“Ce qui est intéressant dans cette étude, c’est la façon dont l’estimation a été construite”, juge El País, qui détaille le repérage par satellite de ces hangars aux systèmes de refroidissement reconnaissables, et note au passage que l’estimation haute “dépasse la consommation annuelle d’un pays comme le Chili”.

Mais l’approche a ses “lacunes”, poursuit le journal espagnol : elle suppose que tous les sites sont raccordés au réseau, objecte Ana Valdivia, de l’université d’Oxford, alors que beaucoup, faute de connexion, produisent désormais leur propre électricité. Les chiffres de Harvard, déjà “stupéfiants”, seraient donc en deçà de la réalité.

items.titel: Krieg gegen die Ukraine: Europas Unterhändler bringen sich in Stellung
items.anriss: Europa hat erstmals mit den USA und Kiew über eine Beendigung des Kriegs diskutiert - und dabei die Vertreter, die später mit Russland verhandeln, instruiert.[ mehr ]

absaetze.t: Europa hat erstmals mit den USA und Kiew über eine Beendigung des Kriegs diskutiert - und dabei die Vertreter, die später mit Russland verhandeln, instruiert.

Europäische Unterhändler haben mit Vertretern der Ukraine und den USA nach Angaben des ukrainischen Präsidenten Wolodymyr Selenskyj sowie des US-Sondergesandten Jared Kushner erste gemeinsame Gespräche zu den Verhandlungen mit Russland über ein Ende des Krieges geführt.

Europa sei bei der Diskussion zum ersten Mal durch diejenigen vertreten gewesen, "die es auch in den Verhandlungen mit Russland repräsentieren werden", fügte Selenskyj hinzu. Konkret nannte er Frankreich, Großbritannien, Deutschland, Polen und Italien sowie Unterhändler der EU und der NATO. Auf ein solches Team hatten sich die Staats- und Regierungschefs der EU am Freitag geeinigt.

Selenskyj erklärte, bei den online geführten Gesprächen seien auch die US-Gesandten Jared Kushner und Steve Witkoff dabei gewesen. "Das Gespräch war nicht einfach, aber es gibt ein Ergebnis", erklärte er, ohne Details zu nennen.
Kushner: Austausch helfe, Lösungen zu erörtern
Kushner bestätigte die Gespräche, an denen seinen Angaben zufolge nationale Sicherheitsberater aus den europäischen Ländern sowie Vertreter der EU und der NATO teilnahmen.

Der US-Gesandte betonte im Onlinedienst X, es gebe "Fortschritte" hinsichtlich einer Beendigung des Krieges. Bei den Beratungen sei vor allem nach Wegen gesucht worden, um "einen direkten Dialog" zwischen der Ukraine und Russland zu "erleichtern". Der Austausch helfe dabei, "mögliche Lösungen zu erörtern und die verbleibenden Differenzen zu überbrücken".

In der vergangenen Woche waren Vertreter Russlands und der Ukraine auf Vermittlung der USA erstmals seit Februar wieder zu direkten Gesprächen zusammengekommen. Bei dem Treffen in Abu Dhabi waren europäische Vertreter nur an der Seitenlinie vertreten. Washington hatte daraufhin erklärt, dass Europa künftig eine "Stimme" bei den Gesprächen haben werde.

items.titel: Nach Huang-Affäre: Bald alles neu in der KI-Chipindustrie?
items.anriss: Konkurrenten wie AMD oder Qualcomm reiben sich nach dem Abgang von Huang als CEO bei Nvidia schon die Hände. Was ist dran am möglichen Umbruch der Chip-Branche - und wie viel hat er tatsächlich mit dem Abtritt Huangs zu tun? Von R. …

absaetze.t: Konkurrenten wie AMD oder Qualcomm reiben sich nach dem Abgang von Huang als CEO bei Nvidia schon die Hände. Was ist dran am möglichen Umbruch der Chip-Branche - und wie viel hat er tatsächlich mit dem Abtritt Huangs zu tun?

Die Zeit des Quasi-Monopolisten ist vorbei, sagen jetzt manche. Für Konkurrenten werde es leichter, ihre KI-Chips auf den Markt zu bringen. Denn das Gesicht der Chip-Schmiede ist weg: Jensen Huang, offenbar vom NVIDIA-Verwaltungsrat vor die Tür gesetzt. Jedenfalls hat Huang seinen Abgang nicht selbst erklärt. Verkündet wurde er vom Verwaltungsrat.

Konkurrenz für Nvidia gibt es schon länger. Doch mit immer neuen Rekordzahlen beherrschte der Konzern bisher die Schlagzeilen. Dabei entwickelt Google schon seit zehn Jahren eigene KI-Chips - und meldet jetzt einen großen Geschäftsabschluss.

Oracle will ab 2027 Cloud-Infrastruktur mit Google-Chips ausstatten. Und OpenAI - bisher nur Mieter in Googles Rechenzentren - plant angeblich, Google-Chips bald auch zu kaufen, für die eigenen Rechenzentren. Insgesamt meldet Google rund 100 Kunden für seine KI-Chips.
Chips von Google als Alternative?

Bemerkenswert findet das KI-Infrastruktur-Spezialist Ben Pouladian vom Tech-Portal The Information: "Großartig, wie Google jetzt seine Chips auch anderen Unternehmen anbietet. Damit hätte ich nie gerechnet. Ich bin wirklich überrascht. Spannend zu sehen, wie aus einem Softwareunternehmen ein richtiger Chiphersteller wird."

Nvidia setzt auf vielseitig einsetzbare Grafikprozessoren mit enormer Rechenleistung. Googles sogenannte TPUs dagegen sind Spezialchips - bei bestimmten Aufgaben effizienter und günstiger. Auch Microsoft und Meta entwickeln eigene KI-Chips. Manche der neueren Spezialchips brauchen nicht einmal Wasserkühlung. Ein wichtiges Argument bei Rechenzentren, deren hoher Wasserverbrauch immer wieder für Kritik sorgt.

Vor allem dort, wo nicht riesige KI-Modelle trainiert werden müssen, können maßgeschneiderte Chips die bessere Wahl sein. Das sagt auch Broadcom-Chef Hock Tan bei CNBC: "Wir entwickeln Chips gemeinsam mit KI-Unternehmen. Deren Entwickler sagen uns, welche Rechenaufgaben sie bewältigen müssen. Und wir entwerfen einen Chip, der genau darauf zugeschnitten ist. So ein Spezialchip ist bei diesen Aufgaben deutlich leistungsfähiger als ein universell einsetzbarer Grafikprozessor."
CUDA bei Nvidia als massiver Vorteil

Broadcom hat unter den klassischen Chipherstellern nach Nvidia sogar einen größeren Marktanteil als AMD. Aber der Platzhirsch hat weiter einen entscheidenden Vorteil gegenüber beiden, sagt Ben Pouladian - da Nvidia mit der Programmierplattform CUDA arbeitet. Das sei ein wesentlicher Unterschied. "Weltweit 100.000 Entwickler verbessern sie fortlaufend. Dazu kommen umfangreiche Softwarebibliotheken für Programmierer."

Schon vor rund 15 Jahren haben Programmierer und KI-Forscher begonnen, diese Schnittstellen ins Innere der Chips zu nutzen. Denn so können die Entwickler - vereinfacht gesagt - den universellen Chips unkompliziert und schnell auch sehr komplexe Aufgaben stellen und später wieder modifizieren. Daraus ist ein bisher kaum einzuholender Vorsprung geworden.
AMD plant Verdoppelung des Rechenzentrumgeschäfts

Doch auch das könnte sich ändern - dank KI selbst, sagt Risikokapital-Experte Umesh Padval bei The Information: "Der Claude-Chatbot ist inzwischen so gut darin, CUDA nachzubilden, dass Start-ups die Nvidia-Plattform nicht mehr unbedingt brauchen." Nvidias Vorsprung beim Software-Ökosystem könnte also schrumpfen. Maßgeschneiderte Chips werden attraktiver. Und AMD rechnet sogar damit, sein Rechenzentrumsgeschäft im kommenden Jahr zu verdoppeln.

Alles eine Folge von Jensen Huangs Fehlern und dem erzwungenen Chefwechsel bei NVIDIA? Eher nicht. Dass Google seine Spezialchips künftig auch an andere Unternehmen verkaufen will, statt sie nur selbst einzusetzen, wurde schon am 27. Oktober bekannt. Die mutmaßliche Spionageaffäre um Jensen Huang erst zwei Tage später. Und solche Chipgeschäfte haben einen langen Vorlauf - oft Monate, manchmal Jahre. Schließlich müssen Technik, Preise, Liefermengen und langfristige Verträge geklärt werden.

items.titel: Le pape Léon XIV conclut sa tournée en Amérique du Sud et rentre à Rome
items.anriss: Le pape Léon XIV s'est envolé lundi pour Rome après une messe géante à Lima, conclusion d'une tournée de douze jours en Amérique du Sud qui a levé les doutes sur sa santé et confirmé la place centrale de la justice sociale dans son …

absaetze.t: Le pape Léon XIV s'est envolé lundi pour Rome après une messe géante à Lima, conclusion d'une tournée de douze jours en Amérique du Sud qui a levé les doutes sur sa santé et confirmé la place centrale de la justice sociale dans son pontificat.

À 71 ans, le premier pape américain, qui possède également la nationalité péruvienne, a parcouru l'Uruguay, l'Argentine et le Pérou, un itinéraire éprouvant, un mois à peine après une opération pour un cancer du poumon.

Au dernier jour de son périple, il a visité un centre pour personnes âgées isolées dans la ville portuaire de Callao, avant de célébrer une messe en plein air sur une base aérienne de la capitale péruvienne, à laquelle ont assisté 1,5 million de personnes selon le Vatican.
En liesse, certains fidèles ont lancé des objets au souverain pontife, qui a reçu dans l'oeil un bracelet religieux sans toutefois interrompre son parcours.
"Le peuple péruvien est aussi mon peuple"

Dans sa dernière homélie avant de regagner le Vatican, Léon XIV a tenu à rendre hommage au pays où il a exercé comme missionnaire puis évêque pendant près de vingt ans. "Le peuple péruvien est aussi mon peuple", a-t-il dit.
"Mon voyage touche à sa fin, mais le temps de la mission continue", a-t-il ajouté.
Selon la spécialiste du Vatican, Elise Ann Allen, le bon déroulé de la visite papale a démontré la "force et la détermination incroyables" de Léon, largement "sous-estimées".
Discours incisifs

Depuis des maisons de retraite et des prisons, dans les Andes ou le bassin amazonien, le chef des 1,4 milliard de catholiques dans le monde a prononcé des discours incisifs et bousculé des dirigeants politiques comme l'Argentin Javier Milei, martelant que la croissance doit bénéficier à tous et prenant la défense des plus vulnérables.

En Uruguay, le souverain pontife s'est aventuré dans le quartier le plus dangereux de la capitale Montevideo pour dénoncer les violences liées au trafic de drogue. Il a également évoqué "la douloureuse réalité du suicide" et exigé le respect des femmes, un thème récurrent durant son voyage dans la région.

En Argentine, Léon a rassemblé plus de deux millions de personnes lors de messes à Buenos Aires et Lujan, les plus massives de son pontificat à ce jour, dans un pays qui a attendu, en vain, le retour de son prédécesseur François, né à Buenos Aires.
"Nouveau chapitre"

À son arrivée au Pérou, pays auquel il a dédié la moitié de son voyage, le pape a été accueilli à son arrivée à Lima par près de trois millions de personnes. Léon XIV a exhorté les Péruviens à surmonter les divisions liées au passé, dans un pays toujours profondément fragmenté par l'époque de l'ex-président Alberto Fujimori, condamné pour des violations des droits humains et père de l'actuelle présidente Keiko Fujimori.

Au Pérou comme en Argentine, Léon XIV a aussi rencontré plusieurs victimes de violences sexuelles commises par des membres du clergé. Évoquant une "réalité qui nous a causé tant de douleur", Léon XIV a appelé à y répondre "par la vérité" et à renforcer la prévention.
À Pucallpa, le pape a dénoncé les menaces qui pèsent sur la forêt tropicale et l'"abandon" des populations autochtones par les autorités, appelant à écouter "le cri" de la terre et des pauvres.

Cette tournée papale a rassuré sur sa capacité à poursuivre la mission confiée il y a un an et demi. "Nous voyons s'ouvrir un nouveau chapitre du pontificat du pape Léon", affirme sa biographe, Elise Ann Allen.

items.titel: Kerch Bridge Struck For The Second Time In Less Than 24 Hours: Russia
items.anriss: Ukraine has launched a second attack on the Kerch Bridge in less than 24 hours. The latest strike on Vladimir Putin’s prized span linking occupied Crimean with Russia was confirmed by the Russian-installed head of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov.

absaetze.t: Ukraine has launched a second attack on the Kerch Bridge in less than 24 hours. The latest strike on Vladimir Putin’s prized span linking occupied Crimean with Russia was confirmed by the Russian-installed head of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov.
“The enemy attacked the Crimean Bridge again,” Aksyonov wrote on Telegram at about 1:34 a.m. local time on Tuesday. “Currently, traffic is suspended.”

“We ask residents and visitors of Crimea to refrain from traveling towards the bridge and to take into account any restrictions when planning their routes,” he added. “We will provide further updates on the situation. Please remember to only trust official sources of information.”

Videos have emerged on social media purporting to show explosions and fire from the latest attack. In particular, one clip shows an explosion in what appears to be the same part of the bridge that was hit before and the bridge losing its shape. However, the poor nature of imagery makes it hard to discern its authenticity or the outcome of the strike if it is indeed real.
So far, no Ukrainian officials have come forward to take credit for the second strike on the Kerch Bridge, which, as we suggested hours ago, would likely happen.

As we noted in our story about the earlier first attack, the extent of the damage from that incident remains unclear, but there were very visible signs of the main road span on the Kerch side of the bridge having been damaged.

Footage broadcast on Russian television first showed significant damage to the crossing. The main road span looks to have sustained a direct hit to its arch, with visible deformation of the structure.

Meanwhile, satellite imagery confirmed signs of damage to the bridge following the first attack, including around the arch of the road crossing, consistent with what we can see in the Russian television report. The imagery also appeared to show dark marks, possibly scorch marks, at the opposite end of the main road span, although these may not be related to the initial attack.
There are indications that the damaged arch was tilted 4.9 degrees after the first attack. Such damage could severely limit the loads the span can safely carry.

The Monday attack marked the first time in more than a year Ukraine struck the bridge after three previous attacks damaged it. The bridge has remained a top target for Ukrainian forces. Beyond its enormous symbolic value as a signature infrastructure project associated with Putin, it provides a critical road and rail connection for moving military personnel, equipment, and supplies between mainland Russia and occupied Crimea.
This is a developing story.
UPDATE: 8:14 PM EST –
Financial Times is reporting that Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko says preliminary reports are that Russian ballistic missiles have hit the northern and southern bridges in Ukraine’s capital.

“Russia has intensified its strikes on Kyiv’s bridges over the Dnipro river in recent weeks,” the publication’s Christopher Miller noted on X. “Ukraine responded last night by hitting the Kerch bridge in occupied Crimea. It seems Moscow decided tonight it would further escalate attacks on the crucial expanses connecting Kyiv and the eastern and western halves of Ukraine.”

“Something new appears to have shifted technologically and/or tactically for Ukraine being able to successfully strike the Kerch Bridge,” TWZ editor-in-chief Tyler Rogoway noted on X. “Unclear what it is, but there has been a new construct here we will probably soon learn about.”
The strikes took place even though, as we previously reported, Ukraine has experienced new disruptions in service from the SpaceX Starshield satellite communications system.
UPDATE: 10:23 PM EST –
Sevastopol residents wanting to head to Russia are being urged not to use the Kerch Bridge.

“The Ukrainian Armed Forces have once again attacked the Crimean Bridge,” Mikhail Razvozhayev, the Russian-installed governor of Sevastopol, said on Telegram. “Traffic has been suspended. I am in constant contact with the Head of the Republic of Crimea, Sergey Valerievich Aksyonov, and we are coordinating our actions and jointly working on all necessary decisions.”

“For those who were planning to leave Sevastopol and travel to mainland Russia via the bridge tonight or this morning, please refrain from traveling for now,” he added. “More information will be available tomorrow morning.”

items.titel: Senate appropriators unveil $1.1T Pentagon spending bill, folding in reconciliation priorities
items.anriss: Nearly $69 billion in money sought by the White House through reconciliation will be rolled into the base budget under the Senate appropriator’s plan.

text.autor: Ashley Roque, Michael Marrow and Carley Welch

absaetze.t: WASHINGTON – Senate appropriators are proposing nearly $1.1 trillion in defense spending for fiscal 2027, a historic figure that includes key priorities but still falls well short of the $1.5 trillion figure sought by the Trump administration.

Until tonight’s release of a proposed spending plan, the Senate Appropriations defense subcommittee was the last of the four defense committees to put forth a budget offering. Now its $1.1 trillion figure will have to be sorted out with a slightly lower topline from its House counterparts. (The Armed Services Committees in the House and Senate both included a topline $1.14 trillion figure, though it is not directly comparable to that of the appropriations committees.)

The Trump administration’s $1.5 trillion ask was split into two categories: $1.15 trillion in the base budget and $350 billion in a reconciliation bill. So far, lawmakers have not moved out with that reconciliation request that funds big-ticket priorities like Golden Dome, critical munitions and the bulk of a $55 billion push for the new Defense Autonomous Warfare Group (DAWG).

The White House has pushed to still pass that $350 billion by reconciliation, but there has been little sign that will happen. According to Punchbowl News, the top Republican in the Senate, John Thune, declined today to say whether a defense-only reconciliation bill is being actively considered.

Senate appropriators are not fans of the reconciliation process, as it takes control of the money out of their hands and gives it to the authorizers. That sentiment was seemingly echoed in a statement from Sen. Mitch McConnell, the defense appropriations subcommittee chair who is retiring at the close of this Congress, who wrote, “This bill is a roadmap to sustainably and responsibly delivering generational investments in the national defense … The nature of warfare is changing, and America’s adversaries are working together to threaten us. Deterring these threats is a project bigger than one-time surges of cash.”
Instead, Senate appropriators are now seeking to funnel some of the Trump priorities into items in their proposal.

“Of this $1.1 trillion, nearly $69 billion, that was initially requested as one-time mandatory spending by the administration, is provided as discretionary funds in order to provide stable, sustainable, and predictable funding for critical capabilities across the Joint Force,” lawmakers wrote in a summary [pdf] of the proposed legislation.

For example, their spending bill includes $9.4 billion for Golden Dome and $3 billion for DAWG; both totals fall far short of the Pentagon’s request, but would be enough keep both initiatives going. The proposed bill includes $47.2 billion to buy munitions with the bulk of the funds, $40.6 billion, directed towards multi-year contracts like Advanced Medium-Range Air to Air Missile, Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement and Precision Strike Missile Increment 1 – key agreements that are in place, in principle, with contractors but have yet to be funded.

Appropriators would also move to rescue other high-priority items like F-35 fighter jets amid dim prospects for a reconciliation bill. Noting that the Trump administration banked on reconciliation to fund 53 jets alongside 32 in its base budget request, appropriators would add roughly half that amount, budgeting an increase of $4.1 billion to buy an additional five conventional takeoff and landing F-35As, five jump-jet F-35Bs and 15 carrier-launched F-35Cs.
Under the SAC’s plan, the Army would see an increase in both procurement and research, development test and evaluation funds, mainly for its aviation programs.

The committee recommended increasing the funding for the Boeing-made Chinook CH-47 helicopters from $210.6 million in the president’s budget to $570.6 million. This is also more than the House committee recommended for the program at $456 million.

The committee also recommended adding $185 million for the Improved Turbine Engine Program which was zeroed out in the president’s budget. The House committee previously recommended $155 million for the program — which aims to field an engine designed to provide a 50 percent increase in horsepower and a 25 percent improved fuel efficiency rate for the service’s Apache and Blackhawk helos.

Regarding counter drone capabilities for the Army, the committee recommended an increase of $150 million for more Coyote Block 2 and Block 3 platforms, but recommended a decrease of $65.6 million for the Enduring-High Energy Laser program, stating it is “ahead of need.”
When it comes to shipbuilding, the Senate panel included $42 billion with $1.9 billion in additional funding for a second DDG 51 destroyer.

To help pay for unforeseen costs, senate appropriators also included $1.7 billion to “mitigate the department’s projected FY2027 fuel shortfall,” along with $1.9 billion in “flexible readiness funding” to address emerging and unfunded requirements.
Next Steps

The Senate spending bill still needs to work its way through the chamber and receive a vote on the floor before Senate and House leaders decide on the next steps for passing a single bill to the president. And Congressional leaders need to sort it all out by Dec. 11, when the continuing resolution funding the government expires; otherwise, they will have to extend the CR or face a government shutdown.

While US President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have continued to publicly push for $1.5 trillion to fund the Pentagon this year, in September the department’s comptroller Jules Hurst told Breaking Defense said he is prepared to work with lawmakers to figure out how to shuffle key priorities.

“If we really want to fund those things, then we have an opportunity to go back to the appropriators before they finalize the bill, at least I think we will…. it’s a conversation, obviously,” Hurst said at the time.

“The question would be, what’s more important to have money for in FY27 [or] can it wait for FY28,” he later added. “And, a lot of these technological areas [are] evolving so fast. Some things we need the money right now to invest in change. … Other things we need to do a little more research and development.”

items.titel: Why Is the Whitney Museum Selling a De Kooning Painting?
items.anriss: Looking to cash in on marquee week in New York, the Whitney Museum of American Art has consigned a Willem de Kooning painting from its collection to Christie's for its 20th-century evening sale tomorrow, November 17. Once a promised gift …

absaetze.t: “Yellow River” (1958) was deaccessioned and will be auctioned at Christie's just three years after it was gifted to the museum in 2023.
November 16, 2026 — 2 min read

Looking to cash in on marquee week in New York, the Whitney Museum of American Art has consigned a Willem de Kooning painting from its collection to Christie's for its 20th-century evening sale tomorrow, November 17. Once a promised gift to the museum, de Kooning's “Yellow River” (1958) is expected to fetch up to $18 million.

The practice of museum deaccessioning has long been a subject of controversy. In 2022, the Association of Art Museum Directors (AAMD) loosened its policy to allow institutions to apply funds from the sale of deaccessioned art toward the “direct care” of their collections.

A lot description for “Yellow River” on Christie's website notes that the proceeds will benefit the Whitney's collection. The Whitney has not yet responded to Hyperallergic's request for comment, but a museum spokesperson told Artnet News that deaccessioning is “a component of the Whitney’s collections strategic plan, allowing the museum to thoughtfully evaluate and refine its holdings in support of its long-term collection priorities.”

The de Kooning painting going under that hammer had a rooted connection to the Whitney before it was bequeathed to the museum in 2023. Postwar art collector, attorney, and museum trustee David Solinger, who would go on to become the museum's first president beyond the Whitney family in 1966, purchased the work from de Kooning's sold-out exhibition at Sidney Janis Gallery in 1959.

“Yellow River” emerged from a series of “highway" paintings representing the artist's shift from cacophonous urban compositions to more airy landscapes, designating the freeway as a conduit connecting New York City to the Hudson River Valley and Long Island's South Fork. In vibrant warm yellow, earthy brown tones, and stretches of deep blue, de Kooning's decisive gestures direct viewers across overlapping paths and visual rest stops throughout the canvas.

“I love to be on those highways,” de Kooning said to British critic and curator David Sylvester about the expansive roads during a BBC interview in 1960. “And they are really not very pretty, but the big embankments and the shoulders of the roads and the curves are flawless.”

“Yellow River” hung at the foot of Solinger's bed for some time, serving as a testament to Solinger's fascination with the artist. His wife, Betty Ann Besch Solinger, took ownership of the work after Solinger passed in 1996, and in 2011, she designated the work as a promised gift to the Whitney in honor of her late husband. It officially entered the Whitney's holdings in 2023, the same year that the museum deaccessioned seven works, including an Edward Hopper landscape, and sent them to auction to benefit the collection.

items.titel: Discover this year's Dezeen Awards Designers of the Year
items.anriss: Dezeen has announced the six winners of Dezeen Awards 2026 Designers of the Year at this evening's ceremony in London, which include Lina Ghotmeh, Keiji Ashizawa and Yinka Ilori .

absaetze.t: Dezeen has announced the six winners of Dezeen Awards 2026 Designers of the Year at this evening’s ceremony in London, which include Lina Ghotmeh, Keiji Ashizawa and Yinka Ilori.
Our Designers of the Year awards recognise the best emerging and established talent whose innovative work has made a notable impact on the industry across architecture, interiors and design.
This year, Ghotmeh took home the architect of the year award, while studio duo Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo were named emerging architect of the year.
Interior designer of the year was awarded to Tokyo-based Ashizawa, and Australian designer Yasmine Ghoniem was named emerging interior designer of the year.
London-based Ilori won designer of the year with Stockholm-based Simon Skinner named emerging designer of the year.
Architect of the year: Lina Ghotmeh

Ghotmeh, who is the founder of architecture practice Lina Ghotmeh Architecture, is one of the world’s most sought-after architects. Among her high-profile projects was the 2023 Serpentine Pavilion and she was recently appointed to renovate the British Museum’s Western Range galleries.
“From Beirut to Paris and beyond, Lina Ghotmeh creates architecture that feels both rooted in history and entirely of the future,” said the judges.

“Her poetic approach to materials, memory and landscape brings buildings to life with a rare sensitivity to people, place and planet. We anticipate her studio continuing to go from strength to strength.”

Ghotmeh is known for her sustainable and historically rooted designs, including the Stone Garden apartment block in Beruit, which was named architecture project of the year at Dezeen Awards 2021. She has received multiple accolades, including being named on the Time100 Next list in 2025 and winning the 2023 Great Arab Minds Award.
Emerging architect of the year: Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo
Founded by Japanese architect Shohei Kuma and French‑Spanish architect and urban designer Elsa Escobedo, Kuma&Elsa is an emerging architecture studio with offices in France, Spain and Japan.

“Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo’s emerging practice brings a fresh sense of curiosity to architecture, balancing bold forms and material experimentation with tactility and unexpected gestures,” said the judges.
“Working between Japan and Europe, Kuma and Elsa are creating an architectural vocabulary that feels both regionally distinctive and deeply connected to its surroundings.”
Among the studio’s varied and intriguing work is Nakano House in Japan’s Fukuoka prefecture – an apartment block informed by the design of a traditional Japanese engawa.
Interior designer of the year: Keiji Ashizawa

Interior designer Ashizawa runs his interdisciplinary, craft-oriented studio based on the ideal of “honest design”. Along with interior spaces, his Tokyo-based studio designs everything from lighting to furniture and products.

“Prolific designer Keiji Ashizawa brings a quiet confidence to interior design, where natural materials, considered details, refined craftsmanship and a sense of calm take centre stage,” said the judges.
“His distinct spaces reveal the beauty in restraint, proving that the most powerful interiors are often those that will quietly stand the test of time.”
Recent work from the studio includes a tea shop in central Shanghai, a holiday home clad in charred cedar in central Japan and a showroom for Japanese furniture brand Karimoku.
Emerging interior designer of the year: Yasmine Ghoniem
Australian designer Ghoniem has found great success since founding her interior studio YSG in 2020 with the aim of creating bold, holistic design experiences.
“Yasmine Ghoniem takes a bold, instinctive approach to interior design, bringing together rich textures, unexpected colour and cultural references,” said the judges.
“Often challenging convention, her interiors are expressive and distinctive, and full of character, warmth and individuality that defy easy categorisation.”

Among her recent – and varied – designs are a wellness hotel in Bali, the revamp of a Sydney apartment, a warehouse conversion in Sydney designed to evoke the Mojave desert and a bar for gin brand Four Pillars.
Designer of the year: Yinka Ilori
Ilori designs pavilions, installations, pop-ups, products and furniture, all united by a bold use of colour informed by his Nigerian heritage.
“Yinka Ilori injects design with an irresistible dose of colour, humour and optimism, turning everyday objects and spaces into lively celebrations of culture and community,” said the judges.

“Rooted in his British-Nigerian heritage, his exuberant work reminds us that design can be as joyful as it is meaningful, bringing people together through shared experiences and bold creative expression.”

Ilori has designed numerous pavilions, including the Colour Palace in London and an events space for the Estrel Berlin hotel in Germany. On a smaller scale, he has designed products including a watch for Swiss brand MB&F and his own range of branded homeware.
He also recently created an extensive collection of furniture, fabrics and homeware for Dunelm.
Emerging designer of the year: Simon Skinner
Swedish designer Skinner is well-known for his furniture, sculpture and installations that explore how materials can be rethought or reused.

“Simon Skinner is a burgeoning talent who brings a fresh perspective to contemporary Scandinavian design, pairing a thoughtful approach to materials with a refined, understated visual language. His work subverts the familiar, creating distinct new objects that hint at an exciting new direction for design.”
Recent examples of his varied, multidisciplinary work include a range of sculptural lights made from second-hand bowls, ashtrays and cat figurines.

Dezeen Awards 2026 in partnership with TrimbleDezeen Awards is the ultimate accolade for architects and designers worldwide. The ninth edition of the annual awards is in partnership with global technology company Trimble. Through connected hardware and software solutions, Trimble helps designers to transform the way they shape spaces and buildings as well as drive productivity in the process. Trimble’s collaboration with Dezeen Awards demonstrates its ongoing commitment to inspiring and supporting creative excellence across the globe.

items.titel: Talking Art and Data With Mona Chalabi
items.anriss: Mona Chalabi is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist, and as much as it shows across her incredible body of visual data reporting, she has always kept her eye on another prize entirely. I sat down with her earlier this fall at Christopher …

absaetze.t: The award-winning journalist and artist talks about her first book. Plus, Carolina A. Miranda on two new Guadalupe Rosales tomes out this fall.
November 16, 2026 — 6 min read

Mona Chalabi is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist, and as much as it shows across her incredible body of visual data reporting, she has always kept her eye on another prize entirely. I sat down with her earlier this fall at Christopher Park across from the Stonewall Inn, a site of protest and resistance, to talk about her new book and her career as a whole.

The culmination of six years of research, interviews, and illustration, Ten Lives breaks the silence around class in her characteristic visual style. To me, it’s a reflection of her principled approach to journalism and storytelling that feel utterly lost in a world where self-promotion, access, and branding can matter more than the work itself. Chalabi brings a refreshing integrity and playful approach to reporting unflinchingly on the genocide in Palestine, the horrors of the healthcare system, and massive wealth inequality. While she insists her work isn’t “fine art,” it’s perhaps the purest example of what art should do: challenge our ways of seeing. She’s also uncommonly funny, humble, and perceptive. (Can you tell I’m a fan?)

Class is also at the center of photographer Mark Alice Durant’s memoiristic book, which critic Melissa Holbrook Pierson likens to Rainer Maria Rilke’s Letters to a Young Poet for our dystopian world of 2026. Other books in this edition similarly respond to the Orwellian state of art and power. Nitasha Dhillon and Amin Husain, both scholars and activists, have organized protests against the Museum of Modern Art in 2021, the Whitney Biennial in 2019, and the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi in 2015, among other instances of artwashing. They penned a joint review of Italian curator and organizer Marco Baravalle’s book The Battleground of Art: Radical Curating in the Crisis of Neoliberalism, a toolkit for seeing through the mainstream art world’s undermining of political movements and building sustainable alternatives.

Critic Carolina A. Miranda, meanwhile, takes up two new books by East Los Angeles artist Guadalupe Rosales, who came up in a community of Chicano kids raised in the 1990s amid uprisings and political action. Miranda writes that the anthology Rosales edited, as well as her blended memoir and photo book, perfectly encapsulate “the ways she engages the stories of others even as she tells her own.” A wise observation to carry with us as we face the week ahead; more of the latest in art book reviews and news below.
—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books

absaetze.t: A tree-top sauna that punctures its architectural framework with the surrounding woodland has been named Dezeen Awards 2026 architecture project of the year following the announcement of all 19 architecture category winners at a party in London.
The 19 winners awarded at the ninth annual Dezeen Awards ceremony are located in 11 different countries, including Canada, France, India, Japan and Mexico.
Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna won the project of the year award in the architecture sector, it was also named leisure and wellness project of the year.
Leisure and wellness projects win big again
The judges hailed the biophilic project as “beautifully minimalist with a spiritual touch of the soul”.
“It’s totally fresh, totally innovative, and never seen before,” they added.
The win marks the second consecutive year that the leisure and wellness project of the year has gone on to claim the overall sector title, following Herzog & de Meuron’s win last year.
Architecture project of the year announced Silent River Tree Sauna by Daichi

The winning project of the year was up against category winners including a sprawling brick-clad university building modelled on stepped wells in India, a country house with walls formed of unstabilised rammed earth in the UK and a project featuring an 18-kilometre-long limestone wall that allows wildlife to pass through in Mexico.

A housing project that appears as if emerging from the natural landscape and a viewpoint designed to evoke a giant silver ring left on the burial site of a legendary Viking were also amongst the category winners.
Architecture project of the year and leisure and wellness project of the year: Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna by Daichi
The project is nestled within a forest in Kanagawa, southwest of Tokyo, and forms part of the Daichi Silent River retreat alongside guest cabins and additional sauna spaces.
The idea for the project was to make the trees feel part of the architecture, using them as both supports and the defining feature of the pared-back structure.
“Leisure and wellness is also about mental health, which this project addresses perfectly,” said the master jury.
“It is a building that offers a spiritual connection between humans and nature.”
House (urban) project of the year: Amami House by Sakai Architects
Local studio Sakai Architects won urban house of the year for its off-grid home on Amami Ōshima, an island in the Amami archipelago off Japan‘s southern coast.
The design was informed by the region’s traditional materials and crafts and its development was spurred by the increase in extreme weather conditions on the island.
“This house shows how we can live sustainably on a small footprint, in close relationship to nature,” the master jury said.
“In a time of climate crisis, it offers an excellent solution for autonomy of energy, while smartly reinterpreting the arrangement and materials of a traditional Japanese house.”
House (rural) project of the year: Jiang Deng Lu by Shisuo Design Office
Shisuo Design Office won rural house of the year for Jiang Deng Lu in Anhui, China.
The compact building is raised partially on stilts to look as though it is floating above its sloped riverside site and made using stainless-steel offcuts salvaged from the client’s own factory.
“This project sits very delicately in its context and is beautiful as a result,” said the judges.
“Innovative in its use of available materials, the project is highly resolved, with incredible quality of light and generosity of space despite a small footprint.”
Housing project of the year: La Querola by Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos
Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos won housing project of the year for La Querola in Ordino, Andorra.
Made up of seven irregularly shaped blocks embedded into the sloping valley and clad in locally sourced slate, the building’s facades feature recessed windows and openings revealing outdoor terraces.
The judges commended the development’s trend-bucking design as a “deliberately expressionist project, celebrating forms that are not repeatable”.
“It’s a deliberate provocation against the salami-type housing where repetition is at the core. It’s unconventional, unique, controversial, and a very strong statement,” they said.
Recently, a fire damaged all seven buildings in the uninhabited development. The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.
House renovation of the year: Haniyasu House by Aatismo
Local architecture studio Aatismo won house renovation of the year for Haniyasu House, a home in the coastal town of Kamakura, Japan.

The project saw the single-storey home, originally built in 1967, stripped back to its timber frame after a typhoon had left it structurally unsound, and boldly characterised with rough walls streaked with clay, soil and metal powders to evoke ceramic glazes.
The judges praised the project’s sensitivity to “the history of both the architecture and its owners”.
“It is aesthetic but also functional, cleverly improving seismic stability,” they added.
House extension of the year: Golmorad by ZAV Architects
Iranian studio ZAV Architects won house extension of the year for its project featuring a series of overlapping arches shifts in colour from terracotta to blue in Tehran, Iran.
Transforming the residence from a weekend villa into a permanent home, its arched series of overlapping arched roofs appears as if organically growing from the home.

The judges found the extension to be “playful with a sense of freedom,” adding that, “it doesn’t manipulate the old house in any way, but instead seems to organically extend it in a very unpredictable direction.”
“It’s clever and fun, with colours that reveal an intent to enjoy life,” they said.
The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.
Civic project of the year: Zando Central Market by Think Tank Architecture
French studio Think Tank Architecture won civic project of the year for its geometric brick-and-concrete market in Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of Congo.

The new building, with space for 20,000 vendors, replaces a historic market on the same site in the capital that was demolished after insufficient maintenance and an overwhelming number of vendors left it unfit for purpose.
“A bold and strong project with really interesting architectural moves, and a capacity to serve the community in a really large-scale way,” said the master jury.
“It has a variety within it to allow a lot of activity to take place, with materials that are simple but sustainable.”
Cultural project of the year: Ismaili Center Houston by Farshid Moussavi Architecture
Farshid Moussavi Architects won cultural project of the year for its Ismaili Center in Houston, United States.

The building and its sprawling gardens is the first Ismaili Center in the US and is one of several around the world commissioned by the current Imam, or spiritual leader, of the Shia Ismaili Muslim community to serve as a place of worship and cultural exchange.
The judges praised it as a “very successful community space that has reinterpreted and reimagined the Ismaili-centric typology in a very contemporary rather than self-referential manner”.
“It has a stunning relationship to light, and incredible detailing and materiality,” they added.
Workplace project (small) of the year: Carpenter’s Home by Primary Architects
Chinese studio Primary Architects won small workplace project of the year for its undulating timber roof-topped studio in Xinyang, China.
The project, a local carpenter’s studio, was designed by the practice to incorporate the craftsman’s studio, as well as a woodcraft workshop that is also open to the public.
“A beautiful project that goes above and beyond the brief,” commended the judges.
“The architecture speaks of its function, offering space that cleverly facilitates different activities.”
Workplace project (large) of the year: Florentia Village by Turner Works
Architecture studio Turner Works won large workplace project of the year for Florentia Village, London.

The practice transformed an old textile manufacturing site in London’s Harringay Warehouse District into a creative hub that offers flexible workshops, studios and industrial units ranging from 46 to 1,400 square metres, alongside community spaces and a cafe.

The judges praised it as “well-thought out in terms of programme, layout and use of materials and colour,” as well as the buildings being “highly flexible, with spaces designed to reinforce a sense of community”.
Education project of the year: Prestige University by Sanjay Puri Architects
Sanjay Puri Architects won education project of the year for its sprawling brick-clad university building in Indore, India.

Referencing traditional stepped wells found in the country, its defining feature is its 9,000-square-metre walkable roof, which comprises 463 stepped platforms that can be used as individual social spaces or as a singular auditorium for up to 9,000 people
“This project creates its own universe,” said the master jury.
“In a country with a tradition of beautiful campuses, but where most new constructions are based on western typologies, this one breaks the mould,” they continued.
“The massing of the roof reduces scale and creates interesting courtyards, creating spaces that feel appropriate for both the place and its climate.”
Heritage project of the year: Olympics Utilities by Chartier-Corbasson Architects
French studio Chartier-Corbasson Architectes won heritage project of the year for its transformation of a neglected underground passage beneath Paris, France.

Located in a passage beneath the Trocadero Gardens, the studio created a public restroom, using an industrial-feeling palette of stainless and weathered steel to highlight its thoughtful, utilitarian design while giving it a new purpose.
“It was a joy to see so much love put into a building typology that we might typically consider unimportant,” said the judges.
“The project creates architectural character, while also preserving a connection to 19th-century futuristic architecture. Unusual, but iconic.”
Hospitality project of the year: Perma by Mold Architects
Perma by Mold Architects in Serifos, Greece won hospitality project of the year, sponsored by Sanderson.

Comprising five guest houses, the rugged retreat on the island of Serifos was constructed by using material extracted during construction to build much of the retreat itself, rather than removing the hillside and building on top of it.
The judges praised its “striking architecture”, noting it as “very innovative in its programmatic possibilities”.
“There is an economy of means in its relationship to the topography, which cleverly reduces the overall footprint,” they said.
Infrastructure and transport project of the year: Naples Underground Central Station by Miralles Tagliabue EMBT
Spanish architecture studio EMBT won infrastructure and transport project of the year for Naples Underground Central Station in Italy.

Contrasting its modernist surroundings with a wavy timber roof, the 10,000-square-metre building was designed to replace a previously understated metro entrance with a new public plaza that felt more integrated with the surrounding city.
The judges commended the project as a “successful urban space, both elegant and spatially interesting.”
“A rich environment to spend time in, not just catch a train,” they continued. “The use of timber is also impressive.”
Small project of the year: Ring of Bjólfur by Arkibygg Architects
Local studios Arkibygg Architects and Esja Architecture won small project of the year for their mountain viewpoint in Seyðisfjörður, Iceland.

Designed to evoke a giant silver ring left on the alleged burial site of a legendary Viking, the viewpoint improves access to a ridge on Mount Bjólfur and celebrates its varied views over the town, valley and surrounding peaks.

The master jury hailed the viewpoint as a “minimal intervention that choreographs the discovery of a landscape in a simple but sophisticated way,” adding that, “the minimal use of material maximises the experience”.
